prize_parts.citation: For the discovery of exact fluctuation relations and the development of stochastic thermodynamics, extending the second law to small systems driven far from equilibrium

statement.case_for: I keep B016 as my preferred single part, but I hold it with a clearer view of its limits after the round-1 exchange. The Evans-Searles and Jarzynski relations are exact statements about the statistics of work and entropy production in systems driven arbitrarily far from equilibrium, and Seifert's trajectory-level definitions of heat, work and entropy turned them into a general framework. They have been checked independently in RNA and DNA pulling experiments, colloidal traps and single-electron devices, and the stable experimental record is now more than two decades long. This is a result about a basic law, the second law at the scale of single fluctuating trajectories, and not a method or a device. Nothing in the round-1 files disputes the physics; the objections to it are about breadth of support and about who is credited. Within a three-person limit I think Jarzynski, Evans and Seifert is the defensible set: Jarzynski for the nonequilibrium work relation, Evans for the first exact fluctuation theorem (with Searles, who is outside the set), and Seifert for stochastic thermodynamics as a framework.
statement.case_against: I have to be direct about the weaknesses. First, I am the only member who prefers B016, and the chair's summary confirms that no one else has it in a preferred configuration; narrow support does not prove the science wrong, but it does make a win unrealistic. Second, the attribution gap is real: any three of Jarzynski, Evans, Crooks and Seifert omit a decisive contributor, Crooks for the detailed fluctuation theorem and the Crooks relation, and Searles and Cohen and Morriss sit behind Evans. I do not think this is smaller than the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap around B044, and I will not claim it is. Third, it is a theory-dominated case without one dramatic observation, and my closeness to the stochastic-process community may flatter it. If the committee votes among the leading candidates, I would put B044 first among them for breadth of confirmed physics, with B024 next if the committee wants cleaner credit.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B044 first, says the Z2 insulators are distinct from the 2016 prize, and concedes that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and three-dimensional credit gap cannot be resolved from the supplied names.
responses.response: I accept the distinction you, Eriksson and Olsson draw, and I move my view of the 2016 overlap: the 2016 citation covered topological phase transitions and quantum Hall-type phases, and a time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulator with no magnetic field is a separate symmetry-protected class with its own experimental signature. That is not a reason for me to discount B044, and I withdraw the suggestion that it should weigh heavily against it. I keep the attribution point, because you describe it yourself as unresolved: a prize that must leave out the proposal that told Molenkamp where to look is no better placed on credit than mine. But I also see that, unlike B016, B044 has broad and deep support and a stable observed phenomenon, so I would now put it ahead of B024 among the alternatives.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is an invention distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, with the cleanest two-name credit, and that a capability gain of about two orders of magnitude is what produces new phenomena.
responses.response: The two-name credit is the strongest feature of B024 and I agree with your answer to the overlap objection: the magic-wavelength lattice with many neutral atoms interrogated at once is a different idea from the comb or single-ion control. Lindroth's point that delivered tests of constants and dark matter so far set limits seems right to me, so I would want the citation to rest on invention and realisation, as Lindroth and the chair ask. I still differ on weight. A more accurate clock is a capability, and a prize committee must decide whether a capability beats an exact law of nature; I put the law first. But I accept that this ordering is a matter of judgement, and I would vote for B024 without reluctance if the committee wants a metrology prize.

responses.point: Lindroth holds B024 first because clean credit matters, treats the 2016 overlap as partly absorbing B044, and agrees that the five-name cold-atom candidate cannot be split.
responses.response: You and I both treat clean credit as a virtue, and the chair asked whether we hold the 2016 reservation for Z2 insulators specifically. For my part I do not: I now think the 2016 prize does not cover them. I did understate the difference in round 1. What remains is only the attribution gap, and I notice that your own argument cuts against B016 as well as B044, since my Crooks problem is not cleaner than the BHZ problem. I therefore concede that a prize cannot rest on conceptual novelty alone when the credited set is contested. What would move me towards B024 over B044 is evidence that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission cannot be handled by citation wording.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B037 to B044 and says the contested three-person selection among Evans, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert is harder to settle than the topological case.
responses.response: The chair's question is whether I will defend B016 as a lead, and your comment is the strongest argument against doing so. You are right that the Evans, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert selection is contested, and a careful committee could reasonably reach a different three. I will give my preferred set but will not insist on it: the choice of Evans over Crooks rests on priority of the first exact theorem, which I think is the stronger ground, though I have not checked the chronology in detail. I also take your point that framing the case as an exact statement rather than a controlled approximation separates B016 from B037, but I concede that DMFT's impact has been very large and that its problem is the same kind of credit problem as mine.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, pairs B024 with a sole-laureate B019 and asks whether any configuration within the supplied credit avoids omitting the AMANDA and IceCube builders.
responses.response: I do not support a sole-laureate prize for IceCube on the supplied credit. The diffuse-flux discovery is solid and I do not doubt it, but a single name for a detector built over decades by a large collaboration leaves out those who built and led it, and the protocol does not let us add names. The same logic applies to my own candidate, so I am not applying a stricter test to you than to myself. A one-part B044 or B024 avoids the problem, and I would support either before a two-part prize that depends on one name for B019.

uncertainties: Whether Jarzynski, Evans and Seifert can be defended against the Crooks and Searles claims; I have not independently checked priority chronology and rely on my recollection of the literature.
Whether the committee will weigh an exact theoretical law with a limited experimental face against the discovery-led candidates. I accept that the opening and round-1 support is narrow.
How much a stable but incomplete credit set (BHZ for B044, Crooks for B016) should weigh against breadth of support; I treat this as a judgement about prize design and not a scientific fact.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My research on stochastic processes is close in subject to B016, but I have no documented collaboration, supervision or institutional tie to Jarzynski, Evans, Seifert or any other credited person on the shortlist. I have no declared relationship to the credited names of B044 or B024 either. I note the subject proximity only as context, and I have not changed this disclosure since round 1.
